title: Sweet Rib Rub
finish: Sugar first, then salt, garlic, and red pepper. A coat that turns mahogany on ribs.
summary: A home sweet rib rub. Sugar leads, salt and garlic behind it, dried red bell pepper in the mix. Pork and chicken.
story: This is the sugar-first rib shaker: white sugar and brown sugar, salt, garlic, onion, sweet paprika for color, dried red bell pepper so it isn't just brown. A pinch of MSG is optional — it's in a lot of the bottled sweet rib rubs and it makes the pork taste louder. Use it on baby backs and spares. Ember House Rub is the balanced house mix. This one is sweeter on purpose.

items: 2 tsp dried red bell pepper flakes (or crushed sweet red pepper)

steps.title: Mix
steps.body:
Break up the brown sugar with your fingers.
Whisk everything until the color is even and you can see the red pepper through it.

steps.title: Jar
steps.body: Airtight jar. Label it Sweet Rib. Keeps 2–3 months.

steps.title: On ribs
steps.body:
Mustard or oil binder. A coat you can still see meat through.
225–275°F. Don't sauce until the last stretch if you sauce at all — this rub is already sweet.

proTips.text: White sugar is the bottled profile. All brown sugar works, but it will taste closer to Ember House Rub.
Skip it if you don't keep it. The rub still works. A teaspoon is the bottled-shaker trick, not a requirement.

milestones.label: On the rack
milestones.hint: Light coat. Sauce late if you sauce.

title: Barbecue Seasoning
finish: Salt first, then garlic and onion, a little sugar. All-purpose.
summary: A home barbecue seasoning. Salt-led, garlic and onion, a touch of sugar. Pork, chicken, vegetables, a steak if you want it.
story: The sweet rib rub is for racks. This jar is the everyday shaker: salt first, then garlic and onion, enough sugar that it browns, not enough that it candies a chicken thigh. Bell pepper and paprika for color. Same optional MSG. Use it when you don't want a dessert crust.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Whisk until the salt and garlic look even. No clumps.

steps.title: Jar
steps.body: Airtight jar. Label it Barbecue Seasoning so you don't grab the Sweet Rib Rub for a steak.

steps.title: On the meat
steps.body:
A light even coat. Chicken, pork chops, vegetables, a burger.
For a long smoke, go easier than the rib rub — this one is saltier.

proTips.text: Sweet Rib Rub is sugar-first. This is salt-first. Don't use them as the same shaker.

title: Sweet Vinegar Sauce
finish: Thin, amber-red, vinegar up front, brown sugar right behind
summary: A sweet vinegar bottle for pulled pork. Cider vinegar, dark brown sugar, a spoon of tomato paste. Not Eastern heat-and-pepper. Not molasses candy.
story: Eastern Carolina vinegar sauce is already in this app — thin, hot, almost no sugar. This is the other vinegar: brown sugar in the pot so it reads sweet, still sharp enough to cut fatty pork. A little tomato paste for color and body, Worcestershire, black pepper, a pinch of red pepper. Toss chopped pork in it. Put the rest on the table. Don't reduce it to glaze.

items: ½ cup packed dark brown sugar

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body:
Everything in a saucepan. Medium-low 10–12 minutes until the sugar dissolves and the tomato paste disappears.
It should stay thin — like a heavy vinaigrette, not Kansas City molasses.

steps.title: Taste
steps.body:
Vinegar first, then sweet. Pepper on the finish.
More brown sugar if you want it sweeter. More vinegar if it sits heavy.
Cool. Bottle. Fridge 3 weeks — vinegar keeps.

steps.title: On the pork
steps.body:
Chop or pull the pork. A ladle of sauce in the pan, toss.
Extra bottle on the table. This is a finishing sauce, not an 8-hour mop.

proTips.text: If you start with a cup of ketchup you made a different sauce. Tomato paste is color. Vinegar is the body.
Eastern Vinegar Sauce in this app is the hot, barely-sweet one. Use that for whole hog. Use this when you want the same tang with more brown sugar.

milestones.label: On the pork
milestones.hint: Ladle in the pan. Extra on the table.

title: Raspberry Chipotle Sauce
finish: Dark raspberry red, sweet fruit first, chipotle on the finish
summary: Raspberry and chipotle in adobo. A glaze for pork, chicken, and a smoked cream cheese. Fruit first, heat second.
story: The bottle people remember from a steakhouse is raspberry jam and canned chipotle. This is that idea, built so it doesn't taste like dessert with a pepper in it. Raspberry preserves for body, a couple peppers from the adobo can, cider vinegar so it cuts fat, a little honey. Strain it if you hate seeds. Brush it on in the last fifteen minutes — sugar burns if you start at hour one.

items: 1 cup raspberry preserves (seedless if you can find them)
½ cup fresh or frozen raspberries
1 Tbsp adobo sauce from the can

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body:
Preserves, berries, minced chipotle, adobo, vinegar, honey, brown sugar, garlic, salt, pepper in a saucepan.
Medium-low 12–15 minutes. The berries collapse and the sauce looks dark red and glossy.
Mash the berries against the side of the pot.

steps.title: Strain or don't
steps.body:
For a steakhouse-smooth glaze, push it through a mesh strainer and throw the seeds.
For a rustic bottle, leave them. Both are right.

steps.title: Taste
steps.body:
Raspberry first. Chipotle on the back of the tongue, not a dare.
More minced chipotle if it's shy. A splash of vinegar if it's candy.
Cool. Bottle. Fridge 2 weeks.

steps.title: On the meat
steps.body:
Thin coats in the last 10–15 minutes on pork ribs, chicken, or a pork loin.
Cold, it's a sandwich sauce and a dip for smoked cream cheese.

proTips.text: Two peppers is friendly. Three is noticeable. The whole can is a different sauce. Taste before you dump.
Preserves are the body. Fresh berries alone make a thin jam that won't stick to a rack.

title: Chicago Mild (and Hot)
finish: Brick-red, celery seed, mild until you stir in the cayenne pot
summary: Tomato, celery seed, a little sugar. The South Side rib-tip sauce. Make one pot mild, pull half, then load the rest with cayenne.
story: In Chicago you do not ask if there is sauce. You ask mild or hot. It is tomato-based, a little sweet, and seasoned with celery seed so it tastes like the Midwest even before the heat. Rib tips and hot links get drowned. White bread is the utensil.

items: For hot: 1–2 Tbsp cayenne and 1 tsp hot sauce, stirred into half the pot

steps.title: Simmer the mild
steps.body: 15–20 minutes until it coats a rib tip but still pours. Celery seed should stay visible.

steps.title: Split for hot
steps.body: Ladle half into a second jar. Cayenne into what's left, simmer 2 minutes. Label them or you will learn the hard way.

proTips.text: Tips come chopped, sauced, on a pile of bread. If you can see a lot of meat, you were shy with the ladle.

milestones.label: Split hot
milestones.hint: Cayenne in half the pot. Label the jars.

title: Maryland Tiger Sauce
finish: Creamy, horseradish-hot, not a barbecue glaze
summary: Mayonnaise and horseradish. The Baltimore pit-beef condiment — punchy, cold, on a Kaiser with shaved rare beef.
story: Tiger sauce is not cooked and it is not smoked. It is the other half of pit beef: mayo, horseradish, a little lemon, enough heat to clear a sinuses next to charcoal-charred round. Put it on the roll, not on the roast while it cooks.

items: 3–4 Tbsp prepared horseradish (more if you are from Baltimore)

steps.title: Stir and wait
steps.body: Horseradish blooms in 20 minutes. Taste. It should make your eyes consider watering. Fridge a few days.

steps.title: On the sandwich
steps.body: Kaiser roll, tiger sauce, a pile of shaved rare pit beef, raw onion. Not a dip for ribs. Not a stand-in for Alabama white, though they would nod at each other.

proTips.text: Bottled 'horseradish sauce' is already mayo. Buy straight horseradish and mix it yourself or it will taste like a steakhouse packet.

milestones.label: Stir
milestones.hint: Horseradish to the edge of polite.

milestones.label: 20-minute bloom
milestones.hint: Then on a Kaiser with rare beef.

title: New Mexico Red Chile
summary: Dried red chile, garlic, oregano. A sauce of chile, not tomato pretending. For pork, lamb, and smoked potatoes.
story: If it tastes like ketchup it is not New Mexico. Toast dried red pods, soak, blend with garlic and oregano, simmer until it coats a spoon. This is what you ladle over smoked pork shoulder tacos and a chuck roast you rubbed with Hatch cumin. Mesquite is optional; the chile is not.

items: 3 oz dried New Mexico or Hatch red chile pods, stems and most seeds out
2½ cups hot water or chicken stock, for soaking

steps.title: Toast and soak
steps.body: Dry skillet, 20–30 seconds a side until fragrant, not burnt. Cover with hot water 20 minutes until leathery-soft.

steps.title: Blend and fry
steps.body: Blend pods with 2 cups of the soaking liquid, garlic, oregano, salt, cumin until smooth. Strain if you want it silky. Fry the puree in lard 5 minutes, then simmer 15 until it thickens. Vinegar at the end.

proTips.text: Canned red chile is a weeknight cheat. If you use it, still fry it in fat and add garlic. Straight from the can tastes like the can.

title: Cajun Butter Mop
summary: Butter, lemon, hot sauce, garlic. The mop for turkey, chicken, and a pork loin that wants a Gulf Coast finish.
story: Louisiana will mop a bird in melted butter, cayenne, and lemon until the skin shines. It is not a tomato sauce. Brush it on in the last 30–40 minutes so the dairy doesn't break into grease for hours. Leftovers make garlic bread that is a problem.

items: 1 tsp Cajun pit rub or paprika plus cayenne

steps.title: Melt, don't brown
steps.body: Butter and garlic on low until fragrant. Off heat, whisk in hot sauce, lemon, rub, Worcestershire. Keep it warm, not simmering.

steps.title: Late on the bird
steps.body: Brush turkey or chicken in the last 30 minutes, two or three thin coats. Earlier than that and you have fried the milk solids into bitterness.

proTips.text: This plus the Cajun rub is a whole program. Skip the KC glaze. The bird already has a personality.

title: Blackberry Pit Sauce
summary: Blackberries, vinegar, a little molasses. The Pacific Northwest bottle for duck, pork loin, and a game bird.
story: Berry sauces go wrong when they taste like cobbler. Keep the vinegar up, the sugar down, and you have something that can sit next to smoked duck or a pork loin without apology. Alder on the meat, blackberry on the side. Not a rib-tip gravy.

steps.title: Simmer and crush
steps.body: Berries, vinegar, water, 15 minutes until they collapse. Mash. Strain if you hate seeds; leave them if you don't.

steps.title: Round it
steps.body: Return to the pot with molasses, sugar, Worcestershire, salt, pepper, mustard. Simmer 10 minutes until it coats a spoon but still pours. Taste for vinegar — it should stay tart.

proTips.text: Marionberries if you can find them. If it tastes like dessert, add vinegar and salt, not more fruit.

title: Mustard Potato Salad
summary: Yellow mustard, pickle, egg. The Texas meat-market salad that belongs next to brisket, not a picnic mayo cloud.
story: Central Texas joints put a mustard potato salad on the tray because fat needs acid and a little crunch. Yukon golds, a hard-boiled egg, celery, dill pickle, and enough yellow mustard that it looks like it means it. Make it a few hours ahead. Serve cool, not fridge-cold to the point of mute.

items: 3 lb Yukon gold potatoes, 1-inch chunks, skin on
2 Tbsp kosher salt for the water
½ cup dill pickle, small dice, plus 1 Tbsp brine
¼ cup minced red onion or scallion
1 tsp paprika, plus more to dust

steps.title: Salt the water like pasta
steps.body: Cover potatoes with cold water, salt it, simmer until a knife slides in with a little resistance — 12–15 minutes. Drain. Spread on a sheet pan 5 minutes so steam leaves.

steps.title: Dress while warm
steps.body: Whisk mustard, mayo, brine, salt, pepper, paprika, celery seed, sugar. Toss with still-warm potatoes so they drink it. Fold in egg, celery, pickle, onion. Taste. It should be sharper than you think — fat from the brisket will calm it.

steps.title: Rest cold
steps.body: Cover, fridge at least 1 hour, up to a day. Dust paprika. Serve from the bowl with a big spoon, not a scoop.

proTips.text: If it tastes like a sandwich spread, you used too much mayo. Mustard is the color and the point.

milestones.label: Dress warm
milestones.hint: Mustard-forward. Fold the pickle and egg.

milestones.label: Cold rest
milestones.hint: An hour at least. Paprika on top.

title: Pit Pickled Onions
finish: Electric magenta, still a little snap
summary: Red onion, vinegar, jalapeño. The jar that cuts through brisket fat when slaw is too much work.
story: Every meat market has a pickle situation. This one is a 20-minute red onion that goes magenta in the brine and lives in the fridge all week. Pile it on sliced brisket, sausage, or a leftover sandwich. Jalapeño in the jar is optional and correct.

steps.title: Pack the jar
steps.body: Onions (and jalapeño) in a clean quart jar, packed but not crushed.

steps.title: Hot brine
steps.body: Bring vinegar, water, sugar, salt, peppercorns, bay to a boil. Pour over the onions to cover. Cap. Cool on the counter 20 minutes, then fridge.

steps.title: Wait a little
steps.body: They're good in 30 minutes, better the next day. Keep a week. The brine also wakes up leftover meat.

proTips.text: If the onions go limp-soggy you sliced them too thin or you boiled them in the brine. Pour hot over raw. That's the whole trick.

milestones.label: Pack the jar
milestones.hint: Half-moons, jalapeño if you want heat.

milestones.label: Hot brine
milestones.hint: Cover, cool, fridge. Magenta by supper.

title: Smoked Cabbage Wedges
finish: Charred edges, tender core, vinegar on the cut face
summary: Cabbage on the pit with bacon and a vinegar mop. The vegetable that actually belongs next to the brisket.
story: A wedge of cabbage will take smoke, bacon fat, and acid without turning into a sermon about eating greens. Quarter it, keep the core so it holds, paint with bacon drippings, and give it 75 minutes next to the meat. Finish with the same vinegar you put on the pork.

items: 1 large green cabbage, cut into 6–8 wedges, core intact
1 Tbsp hot sauce or thin chile mop

steps.title: Render the bacon
steps.body: Crisp the bacon in a skillet. Keep the fat. Mix salt, pepper, garlic.

steps.title: On the grate
steps.body: Brush wedges with fat, season all sides. 275°F, 60–80 minutes, turning once, until the edges char and a knife slips into the core.

steps.title: Vinegar at the end
steps.body: Whisk mop, paint the cut faces, scatter bacon. Five more minutes. Serve the wedges whole — people can pull leaves.

proTips.text: If you shred it first you have made steamed cabbage with extra steps. The wedge is the dish.

milestones.label: Vinegar mop
milestones.hint: Paint the cut faces, bacon on top.
